before.title: Death Wobble (Front Solid-Axle Steering Oscillation)
before.description: Like other coil-sprung, solid-front-axle Jeeps, the XJ is prone to 'death wobble' - a violent, self-sustaining side-to-side shaking of the front axle and steering, usually triggered by a bump or expansion joint at speeds above ~45 mph. It is caused by cumulative slop anywhere in the front steering/suspension system rather than a single part; the most common single culprit is worn track-bar bushings, followed by tie-rod ends and ball joints. Wear accelerates with age, larger tires, or lift kits, and the violent shaking can feel like a loss of control.
before.solution: Inspect the entire front end and replace worn components - most commonly the front track bar (and its bushings/mount), tie-rod ends, ball joints, and control-arm bushings - then confirm proper torque and alignment. A quality track bar, steering-box brace, and fresh steering stabilizer resolve the vast majority of cases. A new steering stabilizer alone only masks the symptom; the worn joint must be replaced.
symptoms: Violent front-end shaking after hitting a bump above 45 mph
Steering wheel shakes hard side to side
Vibration only stops after slowing down significantly

before.title: Cracked Exhaust Manifold on the 4.0L I6
before.description: The factory 4.0L exhaust manifold is well known for cracking, most often where the two down pipes converge into the collector. The cracks are frequently hairline and follow the factory welds; a major cause is that the manifold is rigidly mounted to the chassis while it moves with the engine, stressing the metal. Because the leak opens under load and heat expansion, it is easily mistaken for a lifter/valvetrain tick. Left alone it worsens over time and can also throw off idle quality and cause a slight power loss.
before.solution: Replace the exhaust manifold - many owners fit a heavier aftermarket or upgraded one-piece/header manifold with flex sections to prevent recurrence - along with the manifold gasket and hardware. Welding the factory manifold is generally not worthwhile as it tends to re-crack. Diagnosis is confirmed by a loud tick that appears under acceleration and quiets at idle.
symptoms: Loud ticking/tapping under acceleration that fades at idle
Exhaust smell or tick from front of engine
Slightly erratic idle and minor power loss
Sound resembles a lifter tick but appears under load

before.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor (CPS) Failure Causes Intermittent No-Start and Hot Stalling
before.description: The crankshaft position sensor on the 4.0L I6 and 2.5L I4 XJ is a classic thermal-failure item. Internal components and wiring degrade with age and heat, so the sensor works cold but drops signal once the engine reaches operating temperature. Without a CPS signal the PCM cuts spark and fuel, producing a stall or a crank-but-no-start that mysteriously 'fixes itself' after the engine cools. It is one of the most frequently discussed XJ failures in enthusiast communities and typically strikes around 125,000-175,000 miles.
before.solution: Replace the crankshaft position sensor (mounted at the bell housing / transmission). The 4.0L PCM is notoriously picky about signal quality, so owners strongly recommend a Mopar (OEM) or NTK sensor rather than a cheap generic unit, which frequently causes repeat failures. It is a roughly one-hour job; a scan tool showing loss of RPM signal while cranking helps confirm before replacing.
symptoms: Engine stalls when hot then restarts after cooling

before.title: ZF 9-Speed Transmission Shifting Problems
before.description: The ZF 948TE 9-speed automatic transmission exhibits harsh shifting, delayed engagement, and unexpected shifting into neutral. Early models (2014-2015) experienced the most severe issues. The transmission can unexpectedly shift into neutral while driving, creating a crash risk.
before.solution: Multiple TSB software updates available (TSB 21-013-16, 18-018-17, 21-008-17). For severe cases, transmission replacement or reprogramming required. Always ensure latest software updates installed. Regular transmission fluid services every 60,000 miles recommended.
symptoms: Hanging in 2nd gear before aggressive shift
Transmission suddenly shifts into neutral while driving

Low oil level warnings between oil changes

before.title: Oil Filter Adapter O-Ring Leak (Commonly Misdiagnosed as Rear Main Seal)
before.description: The 4.0L oil filter adapter uses three O-rings that harden and shrink with age (owners describe them becoming brittle 'like bakelite'). When they fail, pressurized oil weeps out and gets blown back onto the rear of the engine, so it is very frequently misdiagnosed as a rear main seal or valve cover leak - compounded by the nose-up engine geometry that makes all oil collect at the RMS area. It is an inexpensive but genuinely common XJ oil-leak source and worth checking before any major RMS teardown.
before.solution: Replace the three adapter O-rings with an oil filter adapter O-ring kit (e.g., Crown 4720363). Note there are two adapter styles - an early hex type and a later Torx type that is harder to access; some owners delete the adapter entirely with a relocation/bypass. It is a low-cost part but requires care to reseal correctly.
symptoms: Oil collecting on rear/side of engine block
Leak appears near the oil filter area
Mistaken for rear main or valve cover leak

before.title: Rear Main Seal Oil Leak (Two-Piece Seal Design)
before.description: The 4.0L is notorious for rear main seal (RMS) leaks, in part due to its two-piece seal design. Compounding the diagnosis, the XJ engine sits nose-up, so oil from almost any upstream leak runs down and collects at the RMS area - the lowest point on the engine - making other leaks look like an RMS failure. A genuine RMS leak leaves oil at the bell housing/flexplate area and can drip onto the driveway over time.
before.solution: Before pulling the transmission, clean the engine thoroughly and rule out cheaper upstream sources (valve cover gasket, distributor gasket, oil pressure sender, oil filter adapter O-rings, timing cover). If the RMS is truly the source, replace it - the seal is inexpensive but labor-intensive because the transmission/flexplate must come off, which drives the cost.
symptoms: Oil drips from bell housing / back of engine
Oil film covering rear of engine and oil pan

before.title: Rear Unibody Frame Rail, Floor Pan and Rocker Rust (Structural)
before.description: The XJ uses a thin unibody with no separate frame, and corrosion is one of its defining long-term problems, especially in salt-belt climates. The rear unibody rails rot where the fuel lines pass through the rail 'tunnel' and near the leaf-spring mounts, while floor pans under the seats/cargo area, rocker panels (which rot from the inside out), and rear quarter panels around the wheel wells also corrode. Because the structure is load-bearing, advanced rust here is a safety/structural issue, not just cosmetic, and can affect leaf-spring mounting integrity. Rust and cracks at the front frame rails/bulkhead welds have also been traced as a cause of death wobble.
before.solution: Cut out all rusted metal and weld in new steel. A large aftermarket ecosystem sells XJ-specific weld-in repair panels for the rear rails, floor pans, rockers, and rear crossmember (Rustbuster, C2C Fabrication, etc.). After repair, treat cavities with rust-inhibiting coatings. Catching it early before it reaches spring/mount points keeps cost far lower.
symptoms: Rust holes in rear unibody rails near fuel lines
Soft/flaking floor pans under seats and cargo area
Rocker panels rotting from inside out
Rust around rear wheel arches and leaf-spring mounts
